blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: No guide of yours covers this subject, so this part was written for the site, as of October 2026. Frontend libraries change quickly: check the official documentation before relying on a detail.

JavaScript looks like Java, which is misleading. The syntax is familiar, while the model is very different.

| Topic | Java | JavaScript |
|---|---|---|
| Types | Static, checked at compile time | Dynamic, checked at run time |
| Numbers | int, long, double, BigDecimal | One `number` type (64-bit float), plus `BigInt` |
| Objects | Instances of classes | Flexible key-value maps with a prototype |
| Functions | Methods in classes | First-class values |
| Concurrency | Threads, shared memory | One main thread, an event loop |
| Null | `null` | `null` and `undefined` |
| Equality | `==` and `.equals` | `===`, and a confusing `==` |
| Execution | Bytecode on a JVM | JIT-compiled in the browser or Node |

### Variables and scope

blocks.code:
const limit = 10;      // can't be reassigned; the common default
let count = 0;         // can be reassigned
var old = 1;           // function-scoped, avoid it

const user = { name: 'Asha' };
user.name = 'Ravi';    // allowed: const fixes the binding, not the object
blocks.title: let, const and var

blocks.text:
`var` ignores block scope, which creates surprising bugs. Use `const` by default, and `let` when you must reassign.

### Types and their traps

| Expression | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `typeof null` | `'object'` | A historic bug |
| `typeof []` | `'object'` | Use `Array.isArray` |
| `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` | `false` | Floating point, as with Java's double |
| `'5' + 1` | `'51'` | `+` prefers strings |
| `'5' - 1` | `4` | `-` converts to numbers |
| `null == undefined` | `true` | A special case of `==` |
| `null === undefined` | `false` | Different types |
| `NaN === NaN` | `false` | Use `Number.isNaN` |
| `[] == false` | `true` | Coercion; never rely on it |

**Always use `===`.** Falsy values are `false`, `0`, `''`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`; everything else is truthy, including `[]`, `{}` and `'0'`.

blocks.code:
const a = 0 || 10;     // 10: || treats 0 as missing
const b = 0 ?? 10;     // 0: ?? only replaces null and undefined

const city = user?.address?.city;   // undefined, rather than an error
blocks.title: Nullish coalescing is often what you meant

blocks.text: Above `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, about 9 quadrillion, integers stop being exact. A Java `long` ID sent as a JSON number can silently change in the browser. Send big IDs as strings. For money, use integer paise or a library, never floats.
blocks.title: Numbers lose precision

blocks.text: ### Objects and arrays, the modern way

blocks.code:
const { name, age = 18 } = user;           // pull out fields, with a default
const [first, ...rest] = [1, 2, 3];        // first = 1, rest = [2, 3]

const copy = { ...user, city: 'Pune' };    // new object with one change
const more = [...rest, 4];                 // new array
blocks.title: Destructuring and spread

blocks.text: Spread makes **shallow** copies, so nested objects are still shared. React relies heavily on these patterns, as you'll see, because it detects change by comparing references.

blocks.code:
const orders = [
  { id: 1, total: 500, paid: true },
  { id: 2, total: 200, paid: false },
  { id: 3, total: 300, paid: true },
];

const paid = orders.filter((o) => o.paid);                  // the Stream filter
const totals = paid.map((o) => o.total);                    // the Stream map
const sum = totals.reduce((acc, t) => acc + t, 0);          // 800
const found = orders.find((o) => o.id === 2);               // first match
const anyLarge = orders.some((o) => o.total > 400);         // true
const sorted = orders.toSorted((a, b) => b.total - a.total); // new sorted array
blocks.title: Array methods replace most loops

blocks.text:
`sort()` changes the array in place, and sorts as strings by default: `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`. Pass a comparison function, and use `toSorted` to avoid mutation.

### Maps and sets

Use `Map` when keys aren't strings or are added dynamically, and `Set` for uniqueness. Note that they compare objects by reference, without any `equals` and `hashCode` to override.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- const by default, === always
- Know the falsy values
- Send long IDs as strings
- Spread copies are shallow
### Functions are values

blocks.code:
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }           // declaration: hoisted
const sub = function (a, b) { return a - b; }; // expression
const mul = (a, b) => a * b;                   // arrow
blocks.title: Three ways to write a function

blocks.text:
Passing functions around is everyday JavaScript, like Java lambdas but without the need for functional interfaces.

### Closures

A function remembers the variables from where it was created, even after that outer function has returned.

blocks.title: A counter with private state

blocks.text: Unlike Java lambdas, closures can capture and change non-final variables. Closures power React hooks, and stale closures are among React's most common bugs. The classic interview question:

blocks.title: var versus let in a loop

blocks.text:
### this

`this` depends on **how a function is called**, not where it's written, unlike Java.

| Call style | `this` is |
|---|---|
| `obj.method()` | `obj` |
| `const f = obj.method; f()` | `undefined` in strict mode |
| `new Thing()` | The new object |
| `f.call(x)` | `x` |
| Arrow function | Whatever `this` was where it was defined |

blocks.title: Losing this

blocks.text:
Function components in React avoid `this` entirely, which is one reason people moved away from classes.

### Prototypes and classes

JavaScript's `class` is syntax over prototypes. An object has a link to another object, and property lookups walk this chain. Classes exist, with `extends`, `super` and `#private` fields, but you'll write far fewer than in Java, as plain objects and functions do most of the work.

blocks.title: A class

blocks.text: ### Modules

blocks.title: ES modules

blocks.text: Imports are like Java's, but each file is a module with private scope. Dynamic `import()` allows code splitting, as Part 9 shows.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Closures capture variables by reference
- this depends on the call
- Arrow functions keep the outer this
- Classes sit on top of prototypes

sections.title: The event loop and asynchronous code

blocks.text: JavaScript runs your code on **one thread**. There's no synchronized, no thread pool to tune, and no shared-memory races in normal code. Instead, long waits are handed off, and callbacks run later.

blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A[Call stack: your code runs here] --> B{Stack empty?}
  B -->|no| A
  B -->|yes| C[Run ALL microtasks: promise callbacks]
  C --> D[Browser may render]
  D --> E[Run ONE macrotask: timer, click, network event]
  E --> A
blocks.title: The event loop

blocks.text: ### Predict the order

blocks.title: A classic interview question

blocks.text: Synchronous code runs first. Then all microtasks, including promise callbacks, and then the next macrotask, such as a timer. A `setTimeout` of 0 means "as soon as possible after this", not "now".

A long loop freezes clicks, scrolling and rendering, as the page uses that same thread. Break up heavy work, or move it to a **Web Worker**, which is a separate thread that communicates through messages.
blocks.title: Blocking the main thread

blocks.text:
### Promises

A promise represents a value that will arrive later, a bit like Java's `CompletableFuture`.

blocks.title: async and await

blocks.text: `fetch` rejects only on network failure. A 404 or 500 still resolves, so always check `res.ok`. Forgetting this is among the most common frontend bugs.
blocks.title: fetch and errors

blocks.text:
### Running things together

| Method | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `await a; await b;` | One after the other |
| `Promise.all([a, b])` | Together; fails if any fail |
| `Promise.allSettled([a, b])` | Together; reports each result |
| `Promise.race([a, b])` | First to settle wins |
| `Promise.any([a, b])` | First to succeed wins |

blocks.title: Sequential or parallel

blocks.text: ### Timeouts and cancellation

blocks.title: Cancel a request that takes too long

blocks.text:
### A race condition, even with one thread

One thread doesn't remove races between async operations. A user types "ja", then "java". If the first search responds last, its old results overwrite the new ones. Solve this by aborting the previous request, or by ignoring responses that aren't the latest. You'll see this again with `useEffect`.

### Events in the DOM

Events **bubble** up from the element clicked to its ancestors, so one listener on a parent can handle many children (event delegation). `event.preventDefault()` stops default behaviour, and `event.stopPropagation()` stops bubbling.

**"How does JavaScript handle concurrency with one thread?"** Your code runs on one thread, while the browser performs I/O and timers elsewhere. Completed work queues callbacks. The event loop runs them when the stack is empty, with microtasks before the next macrotask. Long-running code blocks everything.
blocks.title: Interview answer
Key points
blocks.text:
- One thread and an event loop
- Microtasks run before the next macrotask
- Always check res.ok
- Async races exist: abort stale requests

### Browser storage

| Storage | Size | Sent to server | Lifetime | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cookie | ~4 KB | Yes, automatically | Set by expiry | Sessions |
| localStorage | ~5 MB | No | Until cleared | Preferences |
| sessionStorage | ~5 MB | No | Until tab closes | Per-tab drafts |
| IndexedDB | Large | No | Until cleared | Offline data |

This site's progress and theme use localStorage. Any script on the page can read it, which leads to security.

### XSS

**Cross-site scripting** means an attacker's script runs in your page, and can then do anything the user can.

blocks.code:
{comment}

{/* safe: shown as text */}
{/* dangerous: runs as HTML */} Link {/* check: javascript: URLs are a risk */}
blocks.title: React escapes by default

blocks.text:
If you must render HTML, sanitise it with a library such as DOMPurify. A **Content Security Policy** header adds a second layer, by limiting which scripts can run.

### CSRF

**Cross-site request forgery** tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request, using their cookies. Bearer tokens in headers aren't sent automatically, so they aren't affected in this way. With cookies, use `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict`, and CSRF tokens, which Spring Security supports.

blocks.code: Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
blocks.title: A safe session cookie

blocks.text:
`HttpOnly` stops scripts reading the cookie, `Secure` limits it to HTTPS, and `SameSite` limits cross-site sending.

### The same-origin policy and CORS

An origin is scheme, host and port. Scripts can't read responses from another origin, unless that server allows it through CORS headers. Part 8 covers this with Spring Boot.

### Third-party scripts and dependencies

Every npm package and script tag runs with your page's full power. Keep dependencies few, run `npm audit`, commit your lock file, and be careful with analytics snippets.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- React escapes text by default
- Sanitise any HTML you must render
- HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite on cookies
- Every dependency is trusted code

sections.title: Strings, dates, JSON and regular expressions

blocks.text: ### Strings

blocks.code:
const s = 'Java Trail';
s.includes('Trail');                 // true
s.startsWith('Java');                // true
s.split(' ');                        // ['Java', 'Trail']
s.slice(0, 4);                       // 'Java'
s.slice(-5);                         // 'Trail'
s.replaceAll('a', 'o');              // 'Jovo Troil'
'  hi '.trim();                      // 'hi'
'7'.padStart(3, '0');                // '007'
`Total: ${2 + 3}`;                   // 'Total: 5'
blocks.title: Common operations

blocks.text:
Strings are immutable, as in Java, but compare with `===`, as there's no `equals`.

### Dates

`Date` is a frequent source of bugs. Remember these four facts.

| Fact | Example |
|---|---|
| Months start at 0 | `new Date(2026, 0, 15)` is 15 January |
| Date-only ISO strings parse as UTC | `new Date('2026-10-31')` is midnight UTC |
| Date-time strings with no zone parse as local | `new Date('2026-10-31T10:00')` is local time |
| A `Date` is mutable, and holds one instant | `setDate` changes it in place |

So `new Date('2026-10-31')`, displayed in a timezone behind UTC, shows 30 October. A server-provided `LocalDate` shouldn't go through `Date` at all if you only want to show it. Your Spring API should send instants as UTC, and the browser should format them.

blocks.title: Formatting for people

blocks.text:
`Intl` needs no library. For heavier date maths, use `date-fns`. The new `Temporal` API fixes much of this, once your target browsers support it.

### JSON

blocks.code:
JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: () => 1, c: null });   // '{"c":null}'
JSON.stringify({ when: new Date(0) });     // '{"when":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"}'
JSON.parse('{"when":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"}').when;  // a string, not a Date
blocks.title: JSON traps

blocks.text:
`undefined` and functions vanish, and dates become strings that stay strings. `JSON.parse` throws on bad input, so wrap untrusted strings in `try`.

### Regular expressions

Named groups make long patterns readable: `/(?<year>\d{4})/`. Avoid regular expressions for email validation beyond a basic check, or for parsing HTML. Nested quantifiers such as `(a+)+` can freeze the page on certain input, which is called catastrophic backtracking.

### Iterators and generators

Anything with `Symbol.iterator` works with `for...of` and spread. A generator produces values lazily.

blocks.title: A generator
Key points
blocks.text:
- Months start at 0
- Date-only strings parse as UTC
- JSON drops undefined and functions
- Intl handles most formatting
React sits on top of the DOM, and interviews sometimes ban frameworks. Knowing the plain API also makes you better at debugging React.

blocks.title: The markup
A todo list in plain JavaScript

blocks.text:
Notice how this already resembles React: state, a `render` function, and updates that make new arrays. What React adds is working out the smallest DOM change, which this `render` doesn't do, and so it loses input focus inside rows.

### Events in depth

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[window] -->|capture| B[parent]
  B -->|capture| C[target]
  C -->|bubble| D[parent]
  D -->|bubble| E[window]
blocks.title: Capture, target, bubble

blocks.text:
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `event.target` | The element clicked |
| `event.currentTarget` | The element whose listener is running |
| `preventDefault()` | Stops default behaviour, like submitting |
| `stopPropagation()` | Stops the event travelling further |
| Delegation | One listener on a parent handles children, including future ones |

### Layout thrashing

Reading a layout value such as `offsetHeight` after changing styles forces the browser to calculate layout immediately. Doing this in a loop is very slow.

blocks.title: Read first, then write

blocks.text:
### Browser APIs worth knowing

| API | Use |
|---|---|
| `IntersectionObserver` | Infinite scroll, lazy loading |
| `ResizeObserver` | React to an element's size |
| `MutationObserver` | Watch for DOM changes |
| `requestAnimationFrame` | Smooth animation |
| `navigator.clipboard` | Copy to clipboard |
| `URL`, `URLSearchParams` | Build URLs safely |
| `AbortController` | Cancel fetches and remove listeners |
| `BroadcastChannel` | Talk between tabs |

blocks.title: Build URLs safely
Key points
blocks.text:
- textContent is safe, innerHTML isn't
- Delegate events to a parent
- target and currentTarget differ
- Read layout, then write

### Memory leaks in the browser

The JavaScript engine has a garbage collector, as the JVM does, so the concept is familiar: anything still reachable stays in memory.

| Leak | Example | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Listeners not removed | `window.addEventListener` in an effect | Remove in cleanup |
| Timers still running | `setInterval` with no clear | `clearInterval` in cleanup |
| Growing caches | A module-level array | Limit the size |
| Detached DOM | Holding removed elements in a variable | Drop the reference |
| Closures holding large data | A long-lived callback | Keep closures small |

To find them, use the Memory panel: take a heap snapshot, repeat the action several times, take another, and compare what grew. It's the same idea as a Java heap dump with Eclipse MAT. Single-page apps run for hours in one tab, so leaks matter more than on classic pages.

### Handling errors

blocks.title: Catch what you can handle

blocks.text:
There are no checked exceptions, and anything can be thrown, so `e` may not even be an `Error`. An `async` function's rejected promise, with no `await` or `catch`, becomes an unhandled rejection and often goes unnoticed.

### Node and npm essentials

Node runs JavaScript outside the browser, and your build tools use it even if your backend is Java.

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `npm install` | Installs dependencies, may update the lock file |
| `npm ci` | Clean install, exactly from the lock file |
| `npm run dev` | Runs a script from `package.json` |
| `npx tool` | Runs a package's tool |
| `npm outdated` | Shows newer versions |
| `npm audit` | Reports known vulnerabilities |

blocks.title: Versions in package.json

blocks.text:
`^` allows minor and patch updates, `~` allows only patches, and an exact version allows neither. The lock file records exactly what got installed. `devDependencies` are for building and testing only.

### Bundlers and modules

Browsers can load modules natively, but thousands of small requests are slow, so a bundler combines them. Vite uses native modules for speed in development, and bundles for production. **Tree shaking** removes exports you don't import, and it works best with ES modules, which is why `import { debounce } from 'lodash-es'` can be smaller than importing from CommonJS `lodash`.

Installing a package can run its install scripts on your machine, and malicious packages do appear. Check names carefully, avoid unnecessary dependencies, and commit your lock file. `npm ci --ignore-scripts` reduces risk in CI when your build doesn't need those scripts.
blocks.title: Supply chain risk
Key points
blocks.text:
- Clean up listeners and timers
- Compare heap snapshots to find leaks
- Rethrow what you can't handle
- Use npm ci in CI
#### JavaScript through Java eyes

items.question: What does ['a', 'b'].length + '1' give?
items.answer: The string '21'. `+` with a string concatenates.

items.question: Why might an order ID from your Java API change in the browser?
items.answer: A `long` above about 9 quadrillion can't be represented exactly in a JavaScript number. Send it as a string.

items.question: What does 0 ?? 5 give, and what does 0 || 5 give?
items.answer: 0 and 5. `??` only replaces null and undefined, whereas `||` replaces anything falsy.

blocks.text: #### Functions, closures and this

items.question: Why does a loop with var print 3, 3, 3?
items.answer: There's one shared `i`, and the callbacks run after the loop ends. `let` creates a new binding per iteration.

items.question: Why does passing obj.method as a callback lose this?
items.answer: `this` is set by the call. Called bare, it has no object. Wrap it in an arrow function, or bind it.

items.question: How does a JavaScript closure differ from a Java lambda?
items.answer: It can capture and modify ordinary variables, whereas Java requires effectively final ones.

blocks.text: #### The event loop and asynchronous code

items.question: In what order do a setTimeout(0) and a resolved promise's then callback run?
items.answer: The promise callback first: microtasks run before the next macrotask.

items.question: A fetch to a missing URL returns 404. Does the catch block run?
items.answer: No. fetch only rejects on network failure. Check `res.ok`.

items.question: Search results sometimes show an older query's results. Why?
items.answer: Responses can arrive out of order. Abort earlier requests, or ignore all but the latest.

blocks.text: #### The browser, storage and security

items.question: Why is storing a token in localStorage a risk?
items.answer: Any script running on the page can read it, so one XSS flaw can steal it.

items.question: Why doesn't CSRF affect a bearer token stored in memory?
items.answer: The browser doesn't attach it automatically to requests. Your code does this explicitly.

items.question: How does React protect you from XSS, and what bypasses it?
items.answer: It escapes values in JSX. `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, and `javascript:` URLs, can bypass this.

blocks.text: #### Strings, dates, JSON and regular expressions

items.question: new Date('2026-10-31') shows 30 October for some users. Why?
items.answer: Date-only strings are parsed as UTC midnight, which is the previous day west of UTC. Don't convert a plain date through Date.

items.question: What does JSON.stringify({ a: undefined }) give?
items.answer: `{}`. Undefined values are dropped.

items.question: Which month is new Date(2026, 1, 1)?
items.answer: February, since months start at 0.

blocks.text: #### The DOM without React

items.question: Why add one click listener to a list instead of one per row?
items.answer: Bubbling brings all clicks there, and it also covers rows added later.

items.question: What is layout thrashing?
items.answer: Repeatedly changing styles and reading layout, forcing recalculation each time. Batch reads and writes.

items.question: What's the difference between event.target and currentTarget?
items.answer: `target` is where the event began. `currentTarget` is the element with the running listener.

blocks.text: #### Memory, errors and Node

items.question: A tab gets slower after hours of use. What do you suspect, and how do you check?
items.answer: A leak, such as listeners or timers. Compare heap snapshots after repeating an action.

items.question: What does ^19.0.0 allow?
items.answer: Any 19.x.y version at or above 19.0.0, though the lock file pins what's actually installed.

items.question: Why isn't every error safe to catch and ignore?
items.answer: You hide bugs. Handle what you expect, and rethrow or report the rest.
